He also has her declare her reason in the presence of all the people. Mark's version keeps the doctors who made her worse; Matthew removes the search entirely. Luke makes it a public examination.

wonders.title: Jairus' Daughter Raised
wonders.quote: But He put them all outside, and taking her by the hand, He called, saying, “Child, arise!”
details: Luke notes she was his only daughter, about twelve years old.
Luke adds that the mourners knew she was dead — the ridicule was informed.
Jesus told them to give her something to eat.
wonders.whatHappened: Jairus' only daughter, about twelve, was dying. Word came that she had died and there was no point troubling the teacher, but Jesus told him only to believe. At the house He put the mourners out, took her hand and called her to get up. Her spirit returned, she rose immediately, and He told them to give her something to eat.
wonders.hopeMeaning: Luke says the mourners knew she was dead — their laughter was not ignorance. And still the last instruction is domestic: feed her. The extraordinary ends in someone fetching a meal.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: What ordinary care might be the right response to something you are treating as too big for that?
wonders.distinctive: Luke alone says she was his only daughter, and alone adds that the mourners were ridiculing Him knowing that she was dead — closing off the reading that they were simply mistaken. Mark keeps the Aramaic words; Matthew removes the messengers entirely. Luke sharpens the fact that everyone in the room was certain.

wonders.title: Five Thousand Fed
wonders.quote: They ate and were all filled. They gathered up twelve baskets of broken pieces that were left over.
details: Luke has them seated in groups of about fifty.
The disciples' suggestion was to send everyone away to find their own food.
Five loaves, two fish, twelve baskets left.
wonders.whatHappened: As the day wore on the disciples suggested sending the crowd away to find food and lodging. Jesus told them to give the people something to eat themselves. Seated in groups of about fifty, five thousand men were fed from five loaves and two fish, and twelve baskets of scraps were collected.
wonders.hopeMeaning: The disciples' instinct was to disperse the problem — send them away, let them sort themselves out. They were told to feed them instead, with what they had, which was obviously not enough.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Is there a need you have been hoping will resolve itself elsewhere?
wonders.distinctive: Luke keeps the orderly seating in groups of fifty and sets the whole scene just after the disciples return from being sent out on their own — so the men who have just been given authority are the ones who suggest sending the crowd away. Mark explains the motive as sheep without a shepherd; John names the boy; Matthew counts the women and children.

wonders.title: The Transfiguration
wonders.quote: As He was praying, the appearance of His face was altered, and His clothing became white and dazzling.
details: In Luke it happens while He is praying — that is why they went up.
Moses and Elijah spoke about His departure, which He was to accomplish at Jerusalem.
The disciples were heavy with sleep and nearly missed it.
wonders.whatHappened: Jesus took three disciples up the mountain to pray, and as He prayed His face changed and His clothes became dazzling. Moses and Elijah appeared and spoke about His coming departure at Jerusalem. The disciples were heavy with sleep; when they came fully awake they saw the glory. Peter offered to build shelters, not knowing what he was saying.
wonders.hopeMeaning: It happened during prayer, and the men who came to pray nearly slept through it. Luke does not treat that as scandalous — just true. Being present and being alert are not the same thing, and the glory did not wait for them.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: What might you be sleeping through because it came during something ordinary?
wonders.distinctive: Luke alone gives the reason they went up — to pray — and alone says the change happened as He was praying. He alone reports what Moses and Elijah were discussing: His departure, to be accomplished at Jerusalem. And he alone admits the disciples were heavy with sleep. Matthew has them fall on their faces in terror; Mark has Peter babbling in fear.

wonders.title: The Boy His Disciples Could Not Help
wonders.quote: But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, healed the boy, and gave him back to his father.
details: Luke says he was the man's only child.
The disciples had tried and failed.
Luke ends the sentence by handing the boy back to his father.
wonders.whatHappened: A man begged Jesus to look at his only son, whom the disciples had been unable to help. As the boy came, he was thrown down and convulsed. Jesus rebuked the spirit, healed him, and gave him back to his father — and everyone was astonished at the majesty of God.
wonders.hopeMeaning: Luke's sentence ends with the boy being handed back, the same phrase he used at Nain. Healing in Luke keeps finishing with someone being returned to the person who loves them.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Who would you most want handed back to you?
wonders.distinctive: Luke alone says the boy was an only child — a detail he also gives the widow at Nain and Jairus' daughter — and alone ends with Jesus giving him back to his father. Mark's account is the long one, centred on the father's "help my unbelief"; Matthew's turns to the disciples and the mustard seed. Luke's is the shortest and closes on the handover.

wonders.title: The Woman Bent Double for Eighteen Years
wonders.quote: Ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound eighteen long years, be freed from this bondage on the Sabbath day?
details: She had been bent double for eighteen years and could not straighten up at all.
She did not ask — Jesus saw her and called her over.
The synagogue ruler complained to the crowd rather than to Jesus directly.
wonders.whatHappened: A woman bent double for eighteen years was in the synagogue. Jesus saw her, called her over, told her she was free of it, and laid hands on her — and she straightened up. The synagogue ruler objected to the crowd that there were six other days for healing. Jesus pointed out that they untie an ox on the Sabbath, and asked whether this daughter of Abraham should wait longer.
wonders.hopeMeaning: For eighteen years she could not look anyone in the face. The argument that follows is about whether her freedom could have waited one more day, and the answer is that it could not — the delay itself was the offence.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Is there something you have told yourself can wait a little longer?

wonders.title: The Man with Dropsy
wonders.quote: Jesus, answering, spoke to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?”
details: Jesus was a dinner guest, and was being watched closely.
The man with dropsy was simply there, in front of Him.
He asked the question first, was met with silence, healed the man and let him go.
wonders.whatHappened: At a Sabbath meal in a leading Pharisee's house, where He was being watched, a man with dropsy was in front of Him. Jesus asked the lawyers and Pharisees outright whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath. They said nothing. He healed the man, let him go, and asked whether any of them would leave a son or an ox in a well until the next day.
wonders.hopeMeaning: He asked permission of a room that would not answer, and then acted anyway. The silence did not stop Him, and the man was quietly let go before the argument continued.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: What have you not done because you were waiting for someone to say it was allowed?

wonders.title: Ten Healed, One Returns
wonders.quote: Were there none found who returned to give glory to God, except this foreigner?
details: They stood at a distance, as the law required, and shouted.
They were cleansed as they went, not before they set off.
The one who came back was a Samaritan — a foreigner.
wonders.whatHappened: Ten men with leprosy stood at a distance and shouted for mercy. Jesus told them to go and show themselves to the priests, and they were cleansed on the way. One turned back, praising God loudly, and fell at Jesus' feet — and he was a Samaritan. Jesus asked where the other nine were.
wonders.hopeMeaning: All ten were healed, including the nine who did not come back. The gift was not withdrawn from the ungrateful. What the one who returned received on top of it was being told his faith had made him well.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: What have you received and never gone back to say anything about?

wonders.title: The Blind Man near Jericho
wonders.quote: Jesus said to him, “Receive your sight. Your faith has healed you.”
details: Luke places this as Jesus approaches Jericho rather than leaving it.
He asked what the noise was about before he started shouting.
Afterwards the whole crowd praised God, not just the man.
wonders.whatHappened: A blind man begging by the road heard a crowd going past and asked what was happening. Told that Jesus was passing, he began shouting for mercy, and kept shouting when told to be quiet. Jesus stopped, had him brought over, and asked what he wanted. He received his sight, followed, and glorified God — and all the people praised God too.
wonders.hopeMeaning: He had to ask what the commotion was before he could ask for anything at all. Luke notices that: the man had no way of knowing his moment had come unless somebody told him.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Who tells you when something worth shouting about is going past?
wonders.distinctive: Luke sets it as Jesus draws near to Jericho, where Matthew and Mark have Him leaving it, and Luke alone has the man ask what the noise means before he calls out. Mark names him Bartimaeus and has the cloak thrown aside; Matthew has two men. Luke alone ends with the whole watching crowd praising God.

wonders.title: The Severed Ear Restored
wonders.quote: But Jesus answered, “Let me at least do this”—and He touched His ear and healed Him.
details: This happens during His arrest, moments before He is led away.
The ear belonged to a servant of the high priest — one of the arresting party.
Luke is the only writer who records the ear being healed.
wonders.whatHappened: As Jesus was being arrested, one of His companions struck the high priest's servant and cut off his right ear. Jesus said to let it go that far and no further, touched the man's ear, and healed him — and was then led away.
wonders.hopeMeaning: The last healing before the arrest is done for a man who had come to take Him away, undoing the damage caused by someone defending Him. It is a small, almost invisible act of repair in the middle of a disaster.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Is there damage done on your behalf that you would want to undo?

wonders.title: He Is Risen
wonders.quote: He isn’t here, but is risen. Remember what He told you when He was still in Galilee,
details: Two men in dazzling clothes, where Mark has one young man and Matthew an angel.
The women were told to remember, not simply informed.
The apostles thought it was nonsense and did not believe them.
wonders.whatHappened: The women came at dawn with spices, found the stone rolled away and the body gone. Two men in dazzling clothes asked why they were looking for the living among the dead, and told them to remember what He had said in Galilee. They remembered, went and told the eleven — who thought it was nonsense and did not believe them.
wonders.hopeMeaning: They were not given new information; they were told to remember something they already had. And the people they told dismissed it as idle talk. Being right and being believed are separate matters, and Luke records the gap without softening it.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: What have you already been told that you have simply not remembered?
wonders.distinctive: Luke has two men in dazzling clothes, and alone has them tell the women to remember what Jesus had already said in Galilee — the news is a recollection, not an announcement. He alone records the apostles dismissing the report as nonsense. Matthew has the earthquake and the guards; Mark ends in silence and fear; John follows Mary weeping alone.

wonders.title: Water into Wine at Cana
wonders.location: A wedding in Cana of Galilee
wonders.quote: Everyone serves the good wine first, and when the guests have drunk freely, then that which is worse. You have kept the good wine until now!
details: Running out of wine mid-celebration was a real social embarrassment for the family hosting.
Jesus's mother didn't ask for a miracle — she just told the servants, "Whatever he says to you, do it."
Six large stone jars — roughly 120 to 180 gallons in total — were filled with water, and it came out as wine.
wonders.whatHappened: At a wedding, the wine ran out — a small disaster by any measure, but an embarrassing one for the family hosting it. Jesus told the servants to fill enormous stone water jars, and when they poured a cup out to serve, it had become wine — and remarkably good wine at that.
wonders.hopeMeaning: Not every miracle in this tour starts with someone in mortal danger. This one starts with an ordinary problem on an ordinary day. It shows something worth remembering: the same power that can split a sea is also willing to show up for a wedding that's about to be quietly ruined.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Do you only bring the big crises to God, or is there a small, ordinary worry you've been carrying alone?

wonders.title: The Nobleman's Son Healed from Afar
wonders.quote: Jesus came therefore again to Cana of Galilee, where He made the water into wine. There was a certain nobleman whose son was sick at Capernaum.
details: The boy was about twenty miles away, in another town.
The father wanted Jesus to come down; Jesus did not go.
He checked the time afterwards and found it matched the hour he was told.
wonders.whatHappened: An official came from Capernaum begging Jesus to come down and heal his dying son. Jesus did not go. He told the man his son would live, and the man took Him at His word and set off home. On the way his servants met him with news the boy had recovered — at the exact hour he had been told.
wonders.hopeMeaning: He asked for a visit and got a sentence. He had to walk home for a day on nothing but that, and check the timing afterwards. Belief here came before the evidence, and the evidence came later and matched.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Could you start walking home on a word, before you had anything to confirm it?

wonders.title: The Man at the Pool of Bethesda
wonders.quote: When Jesus saw him lying there, and knew that he had been sick for a long time, He asked him, “Do you want to be made well?”
details: He had been ill for thirty-eight years.
His answer was not yes — it was an explanation of why it had never worked.
It was a Sabbath, and carrying the mat was what got him into trouble.
wonders.whatHappened: By a pool where the sick waited for the water to stir, a man had been ill for thirty-eight years. Jesus asked whether he wanted to be made well. The man did not say yes; he explained that he had no one to help him in, and that someone always got there first. Jesus told him to get up, take his mat and walk. He did.
wonders.hopeMeaning: The question sounds almost cruel until you notice the answer. After thirty-eight years the man no longer answers with what he wants, only with why it has never happened. Being asked what you actually want, after that long, is its own kind of intervention.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: If you were asked whether you want to be made well, would you answer, or explain?

wonders.title: Five Thousand Fed
wonders.location: A hillside on the far side of the Sea of Galilee
wonders.quote: Jesus took the loaves, and having given thanks, He distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to those who were sitting down, likewise also of the fish as much as they desired.
details: The only food anyone could find was a boy's small lunch — five barley loaves and two fish.
More than five thousand people ate until they were full.
Afterward, the leftovers filled twelve baskets — more than they'd started with.
wonders.whatHappened: A crowd of thousands had followed Jesus out to a remote hillside with no food and no way to buy any. A boy offered up his small lunch — five loaves, two fish — and Jesus used it to feed the entire crowd, with baskets of food left over.
wonders.hopeMeaning: The miracle didn't start with abundance. It started with one child's small lunch, offered without knowing what it would become. Hope often begins the same way — not with enough, but with whatever little you actually have, handed over.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: What's the "five loaves and two fish" in your own hands right now — the small thing that doesn't feel like nearly enough?
wonders.distinctive: John alone tells you where the food came from: a boy, and barley loaves — the cheapest bread there was. The other three accounts simply record five loaves and two fish appearing. John also alone keeps the instruction afterwards, to gather the broken pieces so that nothing would be lost. In his telling the miracle begins with a child's lunch and ends with someone being told to pick up the scraps.

wonders.title: Walking on the Water
wonders.quote: They were willing therefore to receive him into the boat. Immediately the boat was at the land where they were going.
details: They had rowed three or four miles into a rising wind.
John's account is the shortest of the three.
The boat reached the shore as soon as they took Him in.
wonders.whatHappened: The disciples set out across the lake in the dark without Jesus. The wind rose and they rowed three or four miles. They saw Him walking on the sea, coming near the boat, and were afraid. He told them not to be. They were willing to take Him in — and immediately the boat was at the land they were heading for.
wonders.hopeMeaning: The rowing stops mattering the moment He is aboard. John gives no rescue scene and no rebuke; the distance simply ends. It is the shortest version and the least dramatic, and it is about arrival.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: What are you still rowing at, that might be closer to shore than it feels?
wonders.distinctive: John's is the briefest of the three and the only one without a resolution inside the men. Matthew turns the night into Peter's walk and rescue; Mark ends on hearts that had not understood about the loaves. John has no Peter, no rebuke, no amazement — only that they were willing to receive Him, and that the boat was immediately where it was going.

wonders.title: The Man Born Blind
wonders.quote: Jesus answered, “This man didn’t sin, nor did his parents, but that the works of God might be revealed in Him.
details: The disciples' first question was whose fault it was.
He had been blind from birth — this was not something that had gone wrong later.
Asked afterwards where Jesus was, the healed man said he did not know.
wonders.whatHappened: Passing a man blind from birth, the disciples asked whose sin had caused it — his or his parents'. Jesus rejected the question, made mud with saliva, put it on the man's eyes and sent him to wash. He went, washed, and came back seeing. When people asked him where Jesus was, he had no idea.
wonders.hopeMeaning: The disciples wanted the cause; Jesus refused to assign one and dealt with the man instead. And the man ends up healed without knowing where his healer went — he did not need to understand the whole thing to have received it.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Are you looking for the reason something happened, or for what to do about it now?

wonders.title: Lazarus Called out of the Tomb
wonders.location: Bethany, four days after the funeral
wonders.quote: "Lazarus, come out!"
details: Jesus arrived four days after Lazarus had died — deliberately, and after his sisters had already sent for him.
Martha's first words to Jesus were part grief, part accusation: "if you had been here, my brother wouldn't have died."
Lazarus came out still bound hand and foot in his grave wrappings, his face wrapped in a cloth — Jesus had to tell the crowd to untie him.
wonders.whatHappened: By the time Jesus reached Bethany, his close friend Lazarus had already been dead and buried for four days — long past any hope of recovery, by every normal measure. Jesus asked for the tomb to be opened, called Lazarus by name, and he walked out alive.
wonders.hopeMeaning: Jesus didn't arrive in time to prevent the death — he arrived after it, on purpose, and grieved it fully before doing anything about it. Hope here isn't the absence of loss. It's what's still possible even after the moment everyone else has already called "too late."
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Is there something in your life you've already decided is too late to hope for?

wonders.title: He Is Risen
wonders.quote: Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to Him, “Rabboni!” Which is to say, “Teacher!”
details: Mary stayed at the tomb weeping after the others had gone home.
She spoke with Him and took Him for the gardener.
What she recognised was not His face but her own name.
wonders.whatHappened: Mary Magdalene stood outside the tomb weeping after the others had left. She looked in and saw two angels, and told them her Lord had been taken away. Turning round, she saw Jesus and did not know Him — she thought He was the gardener and asked where the body had been put. Then He said her name, and she knew Him.
wonders.hopeMeaning: She looked straight at Him and did not recognise Him. What identified Him was not appearance or argument but her name, spoken. And the first thing she is given to do is go and tell.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Is there something you have been looking straight at without recognising?
wonders.distinctive: John narrows the whole morning to one person. Matthew has the earthquake, the angel on the stone and the guards; Mark has the women fleeing in silence; Luke has two men in dazzling clothes and apostles who dismiss the report. John stays with Mary alone at the tomb, weeping, mistaking Him for the gardener — and turns on a single word: her name.

wonders.title: Breakfast on the Shore
wonders.quote: So when they got out on the land, they saw a fire of coals there, with fish and bread laid on it.
details: Peter had gone back to fishing after the resurrection.
They caught nothing all night, and were told to try the other side.
Breakfast was already cooking on the shore before they landed.
wonders.whatHappened: Peter went fishing and several others went with him. They caught nothing all night. At dawn someone on the shore told them to cast on the other side, and the net filled. John recognised Him; Peter threw himself into the water. When they got to land there was already a charcoal fire with fish and bread on it, and Jesus said: come and have breakfast.
wonders.hopeMeaning: He had food cooking before they arrived, and still asked them to bring some of theirs. Peter — who had denied Him beside another charcoal fire — is fed before anything is said about any of it.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Would you let yourself be fed by someone before the conversation you are dreading?

wonders.title: The Day of Pentecost
wonders.quote: They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak with other languages, as the Spirit gave them the ability to speak.
details: They had been told to wait in the city, and had been waiting.
A sound like wind, and something like fire resting on each one of them.
The crowd outside heard their own languages being spoken.
wonders.whatHappened: The followers were together in one place when a sound like a rushing wind filled the house, and what looked like tongues of fire came to rest on each of them. They began speaking in other languages, and the crowd that gathered heard their own native speech coming out of Galileans.
wonders.hopeMeaning: At Babel, language was confused and a people were scattered. Here, language is given and a scattered crowd hears itself understood. The fire rests on each one individually — not on the room, not on the leaders.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: What would it mean to be given something individually, rather than included in something general?

wonders.title: The Lame Man at the Beautiful Gate
wonders.quote: But Peter said, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have, that I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!”
details: He was carried to the gate daily to beg, and had never walked.
He asked for money and was told there was none.
He went into the temple walking and leaping — a place he had only ever been carried to.
wonders.whatHappened: A man lame from birth was carried each day to the temple gate to beg. He asked Peter and John for money. Peter said he had none, took him by the right hand and raised him up in the name of Jesus. His feet and ankles took his weight, and he went into the temple walking and leaping and praising God.
wonders.hopeMeaning: He asked for the small thing he had learned to ask for, because it was all he thought was on offer. What he got instead was the end of the asking.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: What have you learned to settle for asking, because it seems like all that is available?

wonders.title: Ananias and Sapphira
wonders.quote: Ananias, hearing these words, fell down and died. Great fear came on all who heard these things.
details: They sold property and gave part of the money while claiming it was all of it.
Peter points out they were under no obligation to give any of it.
His wife repeated the story three hours later, not knowing what had happened.
wonders.whatHappened: Ananias and Sapphira sold a piece of land and brought part of the money, presenting it as the whole. Peter said plainly that the land had been theirs and the money had been theirs — nobody had required this. The lie was not to men but to God. Ananias fell down and died, and three hours later his wife repeated the story and did the same.
wonders.hopeMeaning: There is no comfort in this account and it should not be given any. What it does say clearly is that nothing was required of them: they could have given a part and said so. The deception was chosen when honesty would have cost nothing.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Is there something you are presenting as more than it is, when the truth would have been enough?

wonders.title: The Apostles Let out of Prison
wonders.quote: But an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors by night, and brought them out and said, “Go stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life.”
details: They were released at night and told to go straight back to public teaching.
They were teaching in the temple by daybreak.
The council sent to the prison for them and found it locked and guarded, and empty.
wonders.whatHappened: The apostles were jailed for teaching. An angel opened the doors at night, brought them out, and told them to go and stand in the temple and keep speaking. By daybreak they were teaching again. The council convened, sent for the prisoners, and found the prison securely locked with the guards at the doors and nobody inside.
wonders.hopeMeaning: They were not freed to go home or lie low. The instruction attached to the rescue was to go straight back to the thing that had got them arrested.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: If you were let out of something, would you go back to what put you there?

wonders.title: Philip Caught Away
wonders.quote: When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away, and the eunuch didn’t see Him any more, for He went on His way rejoicing.
details: Philip had been sent to a desert road for one conversation with one traveller.
The man was a foreigner and a court official reading a scroll he did not understand.
As soon as the baptism was over, Philip was gone.
wonders.whatHappened: Philip was sent to a desert road, where he met an Ethiopian official puzzling over a passage of Isaiah in his chariot. He explained it, the man asked to be baptised, and they went down into the water. Coming up, Philip was taken away — and the man never saw him again, and went on rejoicing.
wonders.hopeMeaning: Philip was sent a long way for one conversation and then removed from it. He did not get to see how the man's life went. Some assignments are complete without ever being followed up.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Could you do something well and then never find out how it turned out?

wonders.title: The Light on the Damascus Road
wonders.quote: He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”
details: He was on his way to arrest followers of Jesus and bring them back in chains.
The question names the persecution as done to Jesus Himself.
He was blind for three days and neither ate nor drank.
wonders.whatHappened: Saul was travelling to Damascus with authority to arrest followers of Jesus when a light stopped him and he fell. A voice asked why he was persecuting Him, and identified itself as the Jesus he was hunting. He got up blind, was led into the city by the hand, and for three days did not eat or drink.
wonders.hopeMeaning: The man arrives in Damascus exactly as he had planned, and is led in by the hand instead of leading others out in chains. The question he is asked is not about doctrine but about who he had actually been hurting.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Is there something you are certain about that you have never examined from the other side?

wonders.title: Saul's Sight Restored
wonders.quote: Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight. He arose and was baptized.
details: Ananias had argued with God about going, having heard what Saul had done.
His first word to him was "Brother Saul".
Afterwards Saul ate and was strengthened, and stayed with the disciples he had come to arrest.
wonders.whatHappened: Ananias was sent to the man who had come to arrest people like him, and said so plainly before going. He went anyway, laid hands on Saul and called him brother. Something like scales fell from Saul's eyes, he could see, and he was baptised — then ate, and stayed several days with the disciples in Damascus.
wonders.hopeMeaning: The wonder needed someone willing to walk into the house of a man who had come to arrest him, and open with the word brother. Ananias objected first and went anyway; both halves of that are in the account.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Is there someone you would have to call brother or sister before you were ready to feel it?

wonders.title: Aeneas Gets up from His Bed
wonders.quote: Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and make your bed!” Immediately He arose.
details: He had been bedridden for eight years.
Peter names Jesus as the one doing it, not himself.
The instruction includes making the bed — the ordinary chore of getting up.
wonders.whatHappened: At Lydda, Peter found a man named Aeneas who had been paralysed and bedridden for eight years. He told him that Jesus Christ was healing him, and to get up and make his bed. He got up at once, and the whole district turned to the Lord.
wonders.hopeMeaning: The instruction includes tidying up after himself. After eight years in that bed, the first act of a restored life is an ordinary domestic chore, and that is treated as the natural thing.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: What ordinary task would mark the end of something for you?

wonders.title: Tabitha Raised
wonders.quote: Peter sent them all out, and knelt down and prayed. Turning to the body, he said, “Tabitha, get up!” She opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter, she sat up.
details: The widows showed Peter the clothes she had made for them while she was alive.
Peter put everyone out of the room before praying, as Jesus had done.
He gave her his hand and raised her up, then called the others back in.
wonders.whatHappened: Tabitha, known for the good she did, fell ill and died. The widows sent for Peter, and when he arrived they stood weeping and showed him the clothes she had made for them. He put them all out, knelt and prayed, and told her to get up. She opened her eyes and sat up, and he presented her alive.
wonders.hopeMeaning: Her memorial, held while she was still lying there, was an armful of clothing she had sewn for people who could not afford it. That is what the room offered as evidence of a life.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: What would people hold up, if they were showing someone what your life had been?

wonders.title: Peter's Prison Doors Open
wonders.location: A prison in Jerusalem, the night before his trial
wonders.quote: an angel of the Lord stood by Him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke Him up, saying, "Stand up quickly!" His chains fell off His hands.
details: Peter was guarded by sixteen soldiers and chained between two of them, the night before he was due to be executed.
He was asleep when the angel arrived — not awake and anxiously waiting for rescue.
The prison's iron gate to the city opened on its own, with no one touching it.
wonders.whatHappened: The night before Peter was due to be publicly executed, chained between two guards inside a heavily secured prison, an angel appeared, woke him up, and simply told him to get dressed and follow. His chains fell off, the guarded doors opened by themselves, and he walked out into the street.
wonders.hopeMeaning: This story happens after Jesus had already died and risen — proof the pattern didn't stop with him. The same kind of rescue that split a sea and calmed a storm kept showing up for ordinary people in impossible, locked situations, long after the Gospels ended.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: What locked door in your life feels the most impossible to open right now?

wonders.title: Herod Struck Down
wonders.quote: Immediately an angel of the Lord struck Him, because He didn’t give God the glory.
details: He had just executed James and imprisoned Peter.
The crowd shouted that his voice was a god's and not a man's.
He accepted it, and the account gives his death in a single sentence.
wonders.whatHappened: Herod, dressed in royal robes, gave a public speech, and the crowd shouted that it was the voice of a god and not of a man. He accepted the acclamation. He was struck down and died — and the account puts it in one sentence, immediately after describing the applause.
wonders.hopeMeaning: This is a judgment account and it is not softened here. It is placed directly after Peter walks out of Herod's prison, and the contrast is the point: the man with all the power is gone within a chapter, and the church he was trying to crush kept growing.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Whose power in your life feels permanent, and probably is not?

wonders.title: Elymas Blinded
wonders.quote: Now, behold, the hand of the Lord is on you, and you will be blind, not seeing the sun for a season!
details: Elymas was actively trying to stop a governor from hearing the message.
The blindness is explicitly temporary — for a season.
He had to be led about by the hand, as Saul had been.
wonders.whatHappened: A magician named Elymas was working to keep the proconsul from listening. Paul looked straight at him, named what he was doing, and said the hand of the Lord was on him and he would be blind for a time. Darkness came over him and he groped about for someone to lead him by the hand. The proconsul believed.
wonders.hopeMeaning: Paul had himself been struck blind on a road and led by the hand into Damascus, and it was the beginning of him rather than the end. The sentence he pronounces here is temporary, and it is the same one he was given.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Has something that stopped you in your tracks ever turned out to be a beginning?

wonders.title: The Lame Man at Lystra
wonders.quote: At Lystra a certain man sat, impotent in his feet, a cripple from his mother’s womb, who never had walked.
details: He had never walked in his life.
He was simply listening — he had not asked for anything.
The crowd's response was to try to offer sacrifices to Paul and Barnabas.
wonders.whatHappened: At Lystra a man crippled from birth sat listening to Paul speak. Paul looked at him, saw that he had faith to be healed, and told him to stand up. He jumped up and walked — and the crowd immediately decided the two men were gods and had to be stopped from sacrificing to them.
wonders.hopeMeaning: He was noticed while listening, not while asking. Something in how he was receiving what he heard was visible from the front of the crowd.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: What might be visible in how you listen?

wonders.title: The Slave Girl Who Followed Paul
wonders.quote: But Paul, becoming greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her!” It came out that very hour.
details: She was a slave whose owners profited from her fortune telling.
What she shouted about them was entirely accurate.
Her freedom ended her owners' income, and they had Paul and Silas beaten and jailed.
wonders.whatHappened: A slave girl who made money for her owners by fortune telling followed Paul for days, shouting — accurately — that these men were servants of the Most High God. Eventually Paul turned and commanded the spirit to come out of her. It did. Her owners, seeing their income gone, dragged Paul and Silas before the magistrates, who had them beaten and imprisoned.
wonders.hopeMeaning: Nobody profits from her freedom except her. The people around her had every financial reason to leave her as she was, and the men who freed her were beaten for it. The account is honest that setting someone free can cost the wrong people money.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Is there something you have left alone because changing it would be costly to someone?

wonders.title: The Earthquake at Philippi
wonders.quote: Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were loosened.
details: Paul and Silas had been beaten and put in the inner cell with their feet in stocks.
They were praying and singing at midnight, and the other prisoners were listening.
When the doors opened, nobody left.
wonders.whatHappened: Beaten and locked in the inner cell with their feet in stocks, Paul and Silas were praying and singing at midnight while the other prisoners listened. An earthquake shook the foundations, every door opened and every chain came loose. The jailer, assuming everyone had escaped, drew his sword — and Paul called out that they were all still there.
wonders.hopeMeaning: The doors opened and nobody walked out. The point of the rescue turned out to be the jailer, who would have died for the escape, and who asked that night what he should do.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Is there an open door you should not walk through, because of who it would cost?

wonders.title: Healing at a Distance in Ephesus
wonders.quote: So that even handkerchiefs or aprons were carried away from his body to the sick, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out.
details: The text calls these special miracles — unusual even by the standards of Acts.
The cloths were work aprons and sweat rags from his trade as a tentmaker.
Paul is not recorded as present for any of these healings.
wonders.whatHappened: In Ephesus, the account says God did unusual miracles through Paul: cloths that had touched him — work aprons and sweat rags from the tentmaking bench — were carried to the sick, and illnesses left them.
wonders.hopeMeaning: The objects involved are working clothes, dirty from a trade. The account does not tidy that up into something more dignified, and it does not require Paul to be in the room.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: What ordinary object of yours has carried more weight than it looked like it could?

wonders.title: Eutychus Raised
wonders.quote: Paul went down and fell upon him, and embracing him said, “Don’t be troubled, for his life is in him.”
details: Paul had been talking until midnight, and kept going.
The young man was sitting in a window and fell three floors while asleep.
Afterwards Paul went back up, ate, and talked until daybreak.
wonders.whatHappened: Paul talked on and on into the night in an upstairs room. A young man named Eutychus, sitting in the window, sank into sleep and fell three floors, and was picked up dead. Paul went down, threw himself on him, and said his life was in him. Then he went back upstairs, broke bread, and talked until dawn — and they took the boy home alive, greatly comforted.
wonders.hopeMeaning: The account is quietly funny about its own preacher: the sermon that went on too long is what caused the accident. Nobody is spared in the telling, and the boy is still restored.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: Can you tell a story about yourself that does not make you look good?

wonders.title: The Viper on Malta
wonders.quote: However he shook off the creature into the fire, and wasn’t harmed.
details: He had just survived a shipwreck and was gathering firewood.
The islanders concluded he must be a murderer being caught up with by justice.
When nothing happened, they changed their minds and decided he was a god.
wonders.whatHappened: Shipwrecked on Malta, Paul was gathering brushwood for the fire when a viper fastened onto his hand. The islanders decided he must be a murderer whom justice had caught up with despite the sea. He shook it into the fire and was unharmed — and they changed their minds and said he was a god.
wonders.hopeMeaning: The islanders go from murderer to god in the space of a few minutes, on the same evidence. What people conclude about you can swing wildly and tell you very little.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: How much weight do you give to other people's reading of your circumstances?

wonders.title: Publius' Father Healed
wonders.quote: The father of Publius lay sick of fever and dysentery. Paul entered in to him, prayed, and laying his hands on him, healed him.
details: This happens while Paul is a prisoner being transported to Rome.
Publius was the chief man of the island, who had taken them in for three days.
Afterwards everyone else on the island who was ill came and was cured.
wonders.whatHappened: Publius, the leading man of Malta, took the shipwrecked party in for three days. His father was ill with fever and dysentery. Paul went in, prayed, laid hands on him, and he was healed. After that the rest of the island's sick came, and were cured too.
wonders.hopeMeaning: Paul is a prisoner under guard, on his way to trial, shipwrecked on an island he never meant to visit. None of that stops the work; the detour becomes the assignment.
wonders.reflectionQuestion: What detour are you treating as an interruption to your actual life?
